results.title: Brain region identification

results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response: The adult Drosophila brain contains multiple types of Kenyon cells. According to the Virtual Fly Brain database, there are [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") subclasses of Kenyon cells, including specific types such as [[KCab-c](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110929 "Open KCab-c in Virtual Fly Brain")(i)](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049111 "Open KCab-c(i) in Virtual Fly Brain"), KCab-c, [KCg-m](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111061 "Open KCg-m in Virtual Fly Brain"), [[Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") of main calyx](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047926 "Open Kenyon cell of main calyx in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"). Additionally, the database summarizes that there are three main subtypes of Kenyon cells: alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, which can be further subdivided into subtypes such as core/surface/posterior, anterior-posterior/middle, and dorsal/main/gamma-s/gamma-t classes. VFB holds extensive data on Kenyon cells, including [31468](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of Kenyon cell") images, scRNAseq data, transgene expression data, and connectivity classes, indicating a substantial amount of information is available on these cells.

results.title: Basic connectivity
results.question: What are the main input neurons to the mushroom body?
results.response: The main input neurons to the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are not explicitly stated in the provided evidence. results.title: Gene expression
results.question: What neurotransmitter do mushroom body Kenyon cells use?
results.response: Mushroom body Kenyon cells use acetylcholine as their primary neurotransmitter, according to the VFB database, which supports this based on neurotransmitter tags indicating Kenyon cells are cholinergic.

results.title: Neuroanatomy
results.question: What brain regions does the antennal lobe connect to?
results.response: The [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") connects to the mushroom body and lateral horn. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database, which states that any antennal lobe projection neuron that sends synaptic output to the mushroom body, and that these neurons generally project to the mushroom body calyx and/or lateral horn.

results.title: Cell count
results.question: Approximately how many neurons are in the adult Drosophila central brain?
results.response: The adult Drosophila central brain contains approximately more than 125,000 neurons, according to the Virtual Fly Brain database, as determined by the VFB query. results.title: Central complex structure
results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response:
The question asks about the main components of the Drosophila central complex and their associated functions. However, the resolved entities provided do not include the central complex, but rather the [common oviduct](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004913 "Open common oviduct in Virtual Fly Brain"). 

According to my general training knowledge, the Drosophila central complex is a structure in the insect brain that has been studied for its role in navigation, locomotion, and spatial memory. It is composed of several distinct substructures, including the ellipsoid body, the fan-shaped body, the noduli, and the protocerebral bridge. These components are thought to be involved in various functions such as spatial orientation, visual processing, and the integration of sensory information (literature, e.g., Wolff et al., 2015; Heinze et al., 2013).

VFB holds data on the common oviduct, with [4](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004913,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of common oviduct") records of parts of the common oviduct available. However, this information is not directly relevant to the question about the central complex.

It is worth noting that the central complex is a well-studied structure in Drosophila neuroscience, and more information can be found in the literature. If you're looking for specific data on the central complex, I can suggest some possible follow-up queries to explore the available data.

results.title: Circuit motif
results.question: Describe the dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs). Which DAN types connect to which MBON types?
results.response:

Regarding the connection between specific dan types and MBON types, the literature suggests that dopaminergic input to MBONs comes from specific dan types. However, the exact connection between dan types and MBON types is not explicitly stated in the available information. 

VFB holds a substantial amount of data related to MBONs, including [993](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of MBON") images, [69](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of MBON") subclasses, scRNAseq data, transgene expression data in [157](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in MBON") records, downstream connectivity classes for MBON in [2788](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for MBON") records, and upstream connectivity classes for MBON in [2077](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for MBON") records. Additionally, VFB has data on dan, including [28](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBgn0039286,expressionCluster "Run in VFB: Clusters expressing dan") clusters expressing dan and [13](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBgn0039286,FindStocks "Run in VFB: Find fly stocks for dan") fly stocks for dan. This wealth of information can be further explored to understand the complex connections between dan and MBON. 

For example, the 2077 upstream connectivity classes for MBON and the 28 clusters expressing dan can be analyzed to identify potential connections between specific dan types and MBON types. Furthermore, the 69 subclasses of MBON can be examined to determine if specific dan types connect to specific MBON types. 

In summary, while the exact connection between dan types and MBON types is not explicitly stated, VFB holds extensive data that can be utilized to investigate this complex relationship.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response: The [LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fva "Open LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") visual neuron type is a lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron. According to the Virtual Fly Brain database, its cell body lies in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind (as described by Wu et al., 2016). The LPLC2 neuron has a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer (Klapoetke et al., 2017). This arrangement allows it to detect looming (expansion) stimuli (Klapoetke et al., 2017). The LPLC2 neuron connects to various neurons, including adult cholinergic neurons, T5c neurons, and transmedullary neurons. VFB holds information on 14 neuron classes, including the LPLC2, with detailed neuron profiles and connections.

results.title: Comparative anatomy
results.question: How does the organisation of the antennal lobe compare between adult and larval Drosophila?
results.response: The organisation of the [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") differs between adult and larval Drosophila. According to VFB, the [adult antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00007401 "Open adult antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") is more elaborated than the larval antennal lobe. The organisation of the antennal lobe in adult Drosophila has approximately 50 glomeruli, whereas in larval Drosophila it has around 22 glomeruli (VFB). VFB holds extensive data on the antennal lobe, including images, neurons with various types of connections to the region, parts and subclasses of the antennal lobe, and tracts/nerves innervating it, with over 17,000 images of neurons with some part in the antennal lobe.

results.title: Morphological similarity
results.question: Are there neurons in the Hemibrain dataset that are morphologically similar to the fru+ mAL neurons described in light microscopy studies?
results.response: The Hemibrain dataset, specifically [JRC_FlyEM_Hemibrain](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_00101384 "Open JRC_FlyEM_Hemibrain in Virtual Fly Brain"), contains neurons morphologically similar to the fru+ mAL neurons, as indicated by the presence of adult fru-mAL neuron information in VFB. VFB holds [97](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=VFB_00101384,PaintedDomains "Run in VFB: Painted domains for JRCFIB2018Fum") painted domains for JRCFIB2018Fum, [43944](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=VFB_00101384,AllAlignedImages "Run in VFB: All images aligned to JRCFIB2018Fum") images aligned to JRCFIB2018Fum, and [2](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=VFB_00101384,AlignedDatasets "Run in VFB: Datasets aligned to JRCFIB2018Fum") datasets aligned to JRCFIB2018Fum, providing a substantial amount of data related to the JRC_FlyEM_Hemibrain dataset.

results.title: Upstream circuit
results.question: What sensory neurons provide input to the fan-shaped body, and through how many synaptic steps?
results.response:
The [fan-shaped body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003679 "Open fan-shaped body in Virtual Fly Brain") receives input from various sensory neurons. According to the literature, these include neurons from the visual, olfactory, and mechanosensory systems (for example, as discussed in  Wu et al., 2013, and  Wolff et al., 2015). However, the exact number of synaptic steps between these sensory neurons and the fan-shaped body is not specified in the information available to me. 

VFB holds data on neurons with presynaptic terminals in fan-shaped body ([102](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003679,NeuronsPresynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with presynaptic terminals in fan-shaped body") records) and neurons with postsynaptic terminals in fan-shaped body ([72](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003679,NeuronsPostsynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with postsynaptic terminals in fan-shaped body") records), which could be used to investigate the synaptic connections of the fan-shaped body. Additionally, VFB has images of neurons with some part in fan-shaped body ([11175](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003679,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in fan-shaped body") records) and expression patterns overlapping fan-shaped body ([1634](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003679,ExpressionOverlapsHere "Run in VFB: Expression patterns overlapping fan-shaped body") records), which may provide further insights into the structure and function of the fan-shaped body.

results.title: Pathway tracing
results.question: Trace a pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the lateral horn. What are the intermediate neuron types and their connections?
results.response:
The pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the [adult lateral horn](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00007053 "Open adult lateral horn in Virtual Fly Brain") involves intermediate neuron types, specifically antennal lobe projection neurons, as stated in the VFB-supported high-level pathway: [olfactory receptor neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005926 "Open olfactory receptor neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") -> antennal lobe projection neuron -> adult lateral horn. These antennal lobe projection neurons receive olfactory input in the antennal lobe and send axons to higher brain centers, including the adult lateral horn. 

VFB holds extensive data on the adult lateral horn, including images, neurons with various types of connections, tracts, and transgene expression data, with over [1661](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00007053,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in adult lateral horn") neurons having some part in the adult lateral horn and [42](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00007053,TractsNervesInnervatingHere "Run in VFB: Tracts/nerves innervating adult lateral horn") tracts/nerves innervating it. For olfactory receptor neurons, VFB contains a large amount of data, including images, subclasses, scRNAseq data, transgene expression, and downstream and upstream connectivity classes, with [19014](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005926,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of olfactory receptor neuron") available images and [92](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005926,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of olfactory receptor neuron") subclasses of olfactory receptor neurons.

results.response: The literature suggests that alpha/beta and gamma Kenyon cells converge on the same [mushroom body output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047953 "Open mushroom body output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") types. VFB holds extensive data on the downstream and upstream connectivity classes for mushroom body output neuron, with [2788](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for MBON") and [2077](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for MBON") records respectively, as well as data on [alpha/beta Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100248 "Open alpha/beta Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") connectivity, which could be used to further investigate the specific mushroom body output neurons that receive input from both cell types.

results.title: Anatomical containment chain
results.question: Trace the anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure. What is each level in the hierarchy?
results.response:
The anatomical containment hierarchy from the [antennal lobe glomerulus DA1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003932 "Open antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 in Virtual Fly Brain") up to the top-level brain structure is: antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum -> adult central brain -> adult brain. This information comes from the VFB database, as indicated by the verbatim text and the reference to VFB. 

VFB holds data on neurons and images related to the antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, including [10](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003932,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1") neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, 10 neurons with synaptic terminals in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, and [911](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003932,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1") images of neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1.

The VFB database also contains information on the synaptic terminals, presynaptic terminals, and postsynaptic terminals of neurons in both the adult central complex and the embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe, which could potentially be used to infer connection strength. results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior, as described by Thomas and Wyman (1984). According to VFB, it has a distinct anatomy, with a large cell body located posterior to the lower protocerebrum, a large descending axon, and dendritic arborization in the antennal mechanosensory and motor center. The giant fiber neuron has a large descending axon and arborizes in the ipsilateral zones A and B of the antennal mechanosensory and motor center. 

VFB holds information on the giant fiber neuron's anatomy and connectivity, including its large cell body, descending axon, and dendritic arborization. The neuron's specific anatomy, connectivity, and available driver lines are also described in the literature, with references to Koto et al. (1981), Namiki et al. (2018), and Sturner et al. (2025). 

For the giant fiber neuron, VFB has available data including [22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") images of DNp01, [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in DNp01, [361](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") downstream connectivity classes for DNp01, and [435](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") upstream connectivity classes for DNp01. Relevant publications on the giant fiber neuron include those by Thomas and Wyman (1984), Koto et al. (1981), Namiki et al. (2018), and others. 

The giant fiber neuron's ID is FBbt_00004020, as stated in VFB. Its large descending axon is several times larger than any other axon in the cervical connective, and it enters the cervical connective via the posterior cerebro-cervical fascicle, as described by Power (1948) and Ito et al. (2014). The neuron receives substantial input from zone A and B Johnston organ neurons, as reported by Kim et al. (2020). 

Overall, the giant fiber neuron is a well-studied neuron with a distinct anatomy and connectivity, and is involved in jump escape behavior. VFB provides a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron, including its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.

results.title: Hypothesis generation
results.question: Based on connectivity data, what neuron types might mediate a connection between the visual system and the mushroom body? Could visual information reach the memory circuit?
results.response: Based on connectivity data from VFB, neuron types such as [ML-VPN2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052139 "Open ML-VPN2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052141 "Open Mt-VPN1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052140 "Open Mt-VPN in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mti](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052142 "Open Mti in Virtual Fly Brain"), [T4ai neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052241 "Open T4ai neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") might mediate a connection between the [visual system](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047735 "Open visual system in Virtual Fly Brain") and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain"). Additionally, adult visual projection neurons are known to mediate this connection, with presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body, as found by the VFB query. The visual system and mushroom body are well-represented in VFB, with [1046](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in visual system") neurons having some part in the visual system and [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") neurons having some part in the mushroom body. This suggests that visual information could indeed reach the memory circuit, which involves the mushroom body. Furthermore, VFB contains data on specific tracts, such as the [adult optic lobe-calycal tract](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00048333 "Open adult optic lobe-calycal tract in Virtual Fly Brain"), that may be involved in this connection. Overall, the available data support the idea that visual information can be transmitted to the mushroom body via specific neuron types and tracts.

results.title: Comparative analysis
results.question: Compare the downstream targets of the two main types of clock neurons (s-LNv and l-LNv). Do they converge on any common target neuron types?
results.response: The downstream targets of the two main types of clock neurons, [s-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch03yp "Open s-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain") and [l-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fws "Open l-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain"), do converge on common target neuron types. According to the VFB database, s-LNv and l-LNv have downstream targets including adult interneurons, cholinergic neurons, GABAergic neurons, glutamatergic neurons, octopaminergic neurons, dopaminergic neurons, and serotonergic neurons. More specifically, the downstream targets of s-LNv include adult cholinergic neurons, adult octopaminergic neurons, and adult serotonergic neurons, while l-LNv targets various neuron types including adult cholinergic neurons and interneurons, as found by VFB. This information comes from a comparison of the downstream targets of s-LNv and l-LNv in the VFB database, which found 17 shared downstream target classes among the compared source classes.
